And yet, when you trace this idea back to its origin, you will not find it anywhere in the mouth of Jesus. You will only find it in the pen of Paul. The textual evidence is irrefutable. The earliest written account we have of the Last Supper is not in any of the four Gospels. It's actually in Paul's first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 11, written around 52 to 54 AD.

**[34:30]** Paul says that Jesus broke the bread and says, "This is my body which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me." And then he says of the cup, "This is the cup of the new covenant in my blood. Do this as often as you drink it in remembrance of me." Now, pay close attention to what's not here. There is no mention of the forgiveness of sins. There's no substitutionary language here. There is no idea that blood is being shed to pay a debt or satisfy divine wrath of some sort. Paul frames it as a memorial service, as a act of remembrance. That's it. And remember, Paul prefaces this passage by bragging that he did not receive his Last Supper statement from the disciples of Jesus, but that this statement I just read was given to him in a private vision from Jesus.

**[35:22]** So, keep that in mind because now we're going to watch what happens as this tradition gets picked up and modified by the gospel writers. Each one begins to add a little bit more theology onto Paul's original made-up story. The Gospel of Mark, which is written about 10 to 15 years after Paul's letters at least, reads, "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many." So, Mark adds the phrase, "poured out for many." So, this is a new addition to Paul's writings, which Paul did not say. But even Mark doesn't say what Matthew says, "for the forgiveness of sins." This phrase comes from Matthew 26:28, which reads, "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins."

**[36:07]** So, there it is. Matthew is the first and only gospel writer to add the phrase, "for the forgiveness of sins" to this Last Supper narrative. Neither of Matthew's sources, Mark or Paul, said this statement. Luke doesn't say it, and John doesn't say it. Only Matthew. And so, if you understand how the Gospels were composed, and with these later writers kind of coming along and building on and editing their sources, you can see this doctrine being constructed in real time, layer by layer. Luke's account is even more interesting because many of the earliest and most reliable manuscripts of Luke don't even include the cup saying at all. The longer version of Luke 22 that most modern Bibles print is widely regarded by textual scholars as a later addition that was not part of Luke's original text. So, wherever we go to look for these blood passages in Jesus, we find known and universally agreed upon interpolations. These are not historically reliable statements, and the Jesus Seminar has pointed this out for decades now.

**[37:11]** And outside of this one interpolated passage, the entire Gospel of Luke contains no blood language whatsoever. And so, we watched the Last Supper tradition evolve from a simple memorial meal that Paul invented to a covenant of blood poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins in Matthew. Everywhere else Jesus preaches about salvation, it is always about good works and keeping the commandments, loving your neighbor as yourself. So, this sudden blood atonement passage out of nowhere at the last minute passes the criterion of dissimilarity. It doesn't make any contextual sense in Jesus's Gospel narrative that at the last second he introduces this new variable. Hey guys, I know I was talking about loving your neighbor and keeping the commandments, but just know it's all about the blood I'm pouring out for you.

**[38:03]** How does that make any sense? And then to make it even more clear, in the first century Nazarene liturgy text called the Didache, which means the teaching of the 12, the Last Supper is pictured as eating the bread in remembrance of how Jesus multiplied the loaves and fed everyone. And the blood was to commemorate the fact that Jesus was of the vine of David. So, it was to commemorate that Yeshua truly was the Davidic Messiah to his original Nazarene followers. So, this blood atonement doctrine was clearly not invented by Jesus. It was gradually constructed by different writers over the course of several decades. Each one layering on more sacrificial theology onto the original passage.

**[38:47]** But, the single most dramatic public act of Jesus' ministry was his cleansing of the temple. "But, you have made it into a den of robbers." Jeremiah 7:11. But, the word for robbers in the Hebrew of Jeremiah is parits, which means murderers or shredders or violent ones. And so, this is the Hebrew word that the historical Jesus would have definitely used in the temple.

**[39:37]** You would only speak Hebrew in the temple, especially if you're quoting a scripture as Jesus does here. And Jesus is unquestionably condemning the sacrificial system. So, what the historical Jesus really said, and how the Jewish people listening to him in the temple would have heard it, was, "You have turned my father's house into a [music] den of murder or violence." This is not a man who believed in the sacrificial system, clearly. This was a man who wanted to dismantle it in front of everyone, and was willing to give his life as a ransom for this cause. And twice in the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus quotes the most anti-sacrifice passage in the whole Bible, Hosea 6:6, which says, "Go and learn what this means. **[40:30]** The clear context of Hosea 6:6 is about animal sacrifice. There is no missing it. And Yeshua literally tells them, "Go back and look. You missed something. But, perhaps the most explosive piece of evidence comes from one of the earliest sources we have of Jesus's sayings, called the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew, which is the original gospel account that the Nazarenes used. And over a dozen church fathers, literally the who's who, all agreed that the first gospel account ever written was written by the disciple Matthew himself in the Hebrew dialect for the sake of the Jewish Christians.

**[41:25]** So, what this means is that Matthew was, as we know, a tax collector, which means he must have been scribally literate enough to have written tax records. But, he was likely fully scribally trained, and so he is the most likely disciple of the 12 to have written a gospel account.
